squirrel-removal.intro: Liberty is a small Pickens County town in the Blue Ridge foothills — rolling, wooded country below the mountains, where the town's older homes stand under big hardwoods and the surrounding ridges and creek bottoms are full forest. Its squirrels are foothills squirrels: gray squirrels in the canopy streets, and in the wooded lots at the town's edges, the night-shift counterpart — southern flying squirrels, gliding from the ridge trees into the soffits of the quieter homes. The two tenants need different reads: grays chew in boldly at the roofline by day; flying squirrels slip through gaps an inch wide and are usually discovered by winter-night noise and the droppings in the attic, months after they move in.
squirrel-removal.extendedBody:
Two squirrels, two inspections

A Liberty call starts by establishing which squirrel the house has, because the jobs differ. Gray squirrel sign is daytime and obvious: chewed entries at the eaves, leaf nests, running at dawn and dusk. Flying squirrel sign is subtle: small droppings in attic corners, faint night scratching, entry gaps at the soffit and roof peak too small for a gray. For grays, we exclude and rebuild the chewed openings in metal, and map the canopy bridges. For flying squirrels — social animals that colony up for winter warmth, sometimes dozens in one attic — the exclusion is a full-perimeter seal, every inch-wide gap found, because a colony closed out of one soffit relocates to the other side of the same roof by morning. Foothills homes on wooded lots get both reads as a matter of course. And the wiring check is not optional in either case: a winter of flying squirrels in an attic is a winter of chewing in the dark, and we document what we find plainly.

faqs.q: We hear faint scratching in our Liberty attic only at night, all winter. What is it?
faqs.a: Flying squirrels are the first suspect on a wooded foothills lot — nocturnal, colonial, and active all winter, gliding in from the ridge trees to a warm attic. The inspection confirms it by the sign: the small droppings, the inch-wide soffit gaps, the latrine corners. Exclusion is a full-perimeter job — every small gap sealed, one-way exits at the active ones — because a flying squirrel colony treats a partial seal as a rearrangement. We will also check the wiring in the colony's area; winter colonies chew, and you should know the state of what is above your ceilings.

faqs.q: How much does squirrel removal cost in Liberty?
faqs.a: It depends first on which squirrel — a gray squirrel exclusion at a few chewed entries is one job; a flying squirrel colony needing a full-perimeter seal of a wooded-lot home is a larger one. We identify the animal by its sign at the inspection, then quote the complete job firmly before work starts. The quote covers the sealing that makes it permanent; on a forested Liberty lot, anything less is a season's rental of the same attic to the same colony.

groundhog-removal.intro: Pickens' groundhogs live in the foothills' banks. The county seat stands below Table Rock in the Blue Ridge foothills, in rolling country where the fields and pastures step down the slopes and every sunny bank above a garden or a pasture is a burrow address. Groundhog systems here undermine barn foundations on the slopes, honeycomb the road banks, and put holes in horse pasture — the call that outranks all others, because a burrow entrance in a galloping field is a broken leg in waiting. The town's older homes add the porch and crawlspace dens, and the creeks running to the Saluda system keep the bottoms stocked. Pickens groundhog work is urgent in pasture, structural at barns, and routine at porches — but it is always the whole system, never the one visible hole.
groundhog-removal.extendedBody:
Pasture priority and the whole system

Pickens work is ranked by risk. Pasture systems come first: we trap the groundhogs working the field and collapse or screen the entrances in the grazed ground, walking the full fence line with the owner because the burrow that matters is the one in the horses' path, and there is always one more than the owner knows. Barn systems come second, with backfill where the tunnels run under the foundation. The closing is the permanent half — a foothills bank is generational groundhog real estate, and an open, emptied system is re-let by the next spring's dispersers as reliably as the seasons turn. Removal runs under the depredation permit for your property. And the calendar is part of the craft: systems cleared in late winter, before the litters, are single jobs; the same bank in June holds a family, takes longer, and costs what the delay was always going to cost.

faqs.q: How much does groundhog removal cost in Pickens?
faqs.a: It depends on the system and the ground — a porch den in town is compact; a pasture bank with multiple entrances and a barn foundation to protect is a programme with backfill in the quote. We walk the property first, rank the systems by risk, and give one firm price for the trapping and closing together. On horse properties we treat the first walk as urgent business and will tell you on the phone which precautions to take with the field until we get there.

faqs.q: We keep filling groundhog holes in our Pickens pasture and they keep reopening. What are we doing wrong?
faqs.a: Filling treats the entrance; the tenant treats it as housekeeping. An occupied system is re-excavated from inside within days — groundhogs maintain their burrows as a matter of survival. The sequence that works is the reverse: trap the residents first, then collapse and close the system while it is empty. Filling after removal holds, because what reopens a burrow is a groundhog, and the address has been taken off the market. We will also walk the bank with you — pasture systems often have a second entrance line in the brush that the filling never reached, and that is usually the real story.
